21:A project's run targets are the ways it can be run, each a name and a shell command, run in the project directory: for a Rust project, "Run" as `cargo run`, "Build" as `cargo build`, and "Test" as `cargo test`; for a C++ project built with CMake, "Run" as configuring and building with `cmake`, then running the binary it built; and so on for whatever the project is.
61:success colour, "Exited with N" in its error colour, or "Stopped". Beneath it, its command, muted, in the monospace font, and then what it prints, its output and its errors together, in the order they come, a line each, in the monospace font on the theme's well surface, errors not told apart. The output is clean, as a terminal would show it, as the [RunTargetsShape.consoleOutput](./index.md#console-output-1) says. It scrolls with a [ScrollbarScope](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope) whose lock to the bottom starts on, following the latest output. The well runs beneath its scroll column too, so the column sits on the log's own surface, not the panel's base. A "Stop" button in the header stops it, and every process it started with it, while it runs; once it is over, a "Run again" button runs it afresh in its place.
65:One target runs at a time. Pressing the button of the target running brings back its panel. Pressing another's stops the one running and runs the other in its place. Finding the targets while one runs stops it.
69:Its minimize button's tooltip says the target keeps running, or that the search keeps going. While it runs, it is listed among the [RunningActivityScope](../running-activity/index.md#running-activity-scope), as "Running" then the target's name, or "Finding how to run". Closing the panel stops whatever it holds.
79:carrying on in the background, and switching back brings it back minimized, just as it was left, the Code tab showing that project's targets and which of them runs. Each open project can run one target of its own at a time. Quitting doesn't ask, and stops every target running.
83:What a target prints is shown as a terminal would show it, never as the bytes it wrote. Its terminal escape sequences, those that colour text, move the cursor, clear the line, or set the window's title or a link, never show as text; neither do other control characters, nor bytes that aren't text. A line written over with a carriage return, as a progress bar is, shows as it was last written, a backspace takes back the character before it, and a tab lines up with the next tab stop, four columns along.

input.new_string:
"Run again" button runs it afresh in its place.

        stopping:
            Stopping a target stops everything it started, however deep: the
            shell its command runs in, what the shell runs, and every process
            those start in turn, as a `npm run dev` runs npm, which runs node,
            which runs Vite and its esbuild, or a `cargo run` runs the binary
            it built. A server a target starts, a dev server, a watcher, or
            anything listening on a port, is stopped with it, so its port is
            free once the target reads "Stopped", and running it again never
            fails for the port being taken by the run before. Nothing it
            started is left running, nor left behind as an orphan of the
            shell, whatever the platform.

            So a target's command is started as the head of a process group
            of its own on macOS and Linux, a new session, and on Windows in a
            job object that every process it starts belongs to, its children's
            children included. Stopping it first asks the whole group or job
            to end, as Ctrl+C in a terminal would, SIGINT and then SIGTERM to
            the process group on macOS and Linux, and on Windows a Ctrl+Break
            to its console group, so a server can shut down cleanly; whatever
            is still running 3 seconds later is killed outright, SIGKILL to
            the group on macOS and Linux, and the job terminated on Windows.
            A process that left the group on its own, as one that starts a
            session of its own, is found among the target's descendants and
            stopped the same way.

            The target reads "Stopped" only once every process it started has
            exited, and its Stop button shows a spinner and is disabled until
            then, so "Stopped" always means nothing of it is still running.
            Stopping it the other ways, by running another target in its
            place, finding the targets, closing its panel, or quitting, stops
            it just the same, and quitting doesn't leave a process of it
            running after Suspense has gone. A target that ends by itself,
            as when its command exits, leaves nothing it started running
            either: what is left of its group is stopped as above.

use /lib
use /ui
from /scope/harness-integration/baked-prompts import BakedSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/harness-integration/one-off-run import OneOffAgentRunScope
from /scope/no-project import NoProjectStateScope
from /scope/open-projects import OpenProjectsScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/running-activity import RunningActivityScope
from /ui/components/minimizable-panel import MinimizablePanelScope
from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
from /ui/components/task-table import TaskTableScope
from /ui/theme import ThemeScope

export ui-component RunTargetsScope:
    concept: {RunTargetsConcept}

concept RunTargetsConcept:
    pitch:
        Makes the project runnable from the application, whatever kind of
        project it is: the harness finds out once how the project is built,
        run, and tested, that understanding is saved with the project, and
        each way of running it becomes a button in the ribbon's Code tab.

    shape: {RunTargetsShape}

shape RunTargetsShape:
    description:
        A project's run targets are the ways it can be run, each a name and a
        shell command, run in the project directory: for a Rust project,
        "Run" as `cargo run`, "Build" as `cargo build`, and "Test" as
        `cargo test`; for a C++ project built with CMake, "Run" as configuring
        and building with `cmake`, then running the binary it built; and so
        on for whatever the project is.

    kinds:
        Each target is of a kind, which picks its icon:
        - run, which runs the project, with a play icon
        - build, which only builds it, with a hammer icon
        - test, which runs its tests, with a flask icon
        - other, anything else, with a terminal icon

        A run target can also be marked release: it runs the project from an
        optimized release build, such as `cargo run --release`, rather than
        the build it is developed with. At most one target is marked release.

    finding:
        overview:
            Nothing about a project's targets is guessed by the application
            itself. Finding them is agentic: a @{OneOffAgentRunScope}, whose
            prompt is run-targets.pi, of the @{BakedSystemPromptsScope}, looks
            through the project, its build files, manifests, and readme, and
            replies with its targets, the way to run the project first. Its
            command runs the project from scratch, building first when it has
            to, so it works on a fresh clone.

        saving:
            Once found, the targets are saved with the project's data, as the
            @{ProjectDataScope} says, in run.json, and read from there from then
            on, every time the project is opened: they aren't found again
            unless asked. run.json is kept with the project, so everyone
            working on it has the same buttons, and can be edited by hand; one
            that can't be read counts as no targets found.

        reply:
            The harness replies with JSON listing each target's name, command,
            and kind, and whether it is the release run. Where the project has
            a release build, it adds a release run target, named "Run Release"
            or the like, after the way to run it. A target with no name or no
            command is left out, as is a kind that isn't one of the four, which
            counts as other. Past the first target marked release, none is. A
            reply with no targets at all fails, saving nothing.

    panel:
        overview:
            Finding and running are shown in one @{MinimizablePanelScope},
            titled "Run", which holds one thing at a time: finding the targets,
            or running one of them.

            Whatever the panel holds, its body is inset by the same 16 pixels
            on every side, the top included: the output of a search for its
            targets, the targets found, and a target's output all start 16
            pixels below the line above them, never flush against it, and end
            16 pixels above the panel's bottom once scrolled to their end.

        whileFinding:
            While finding, the panel shows a step, "Looking at the project",
            with a spinner while it runs, a tick once done, or a cross and why
            if it failed, and beneath it the run's output in its
            @{TaskTableScope}. Once found, in its place, the targets found, one
            row each: its icon, its name, and its command, muted, in the
            editor's monospace font, beneath a line saying they were saved to
            .suspense/run.json and that the Code tab has a button for each. A
            failure keeps whatever targets were saved before. "Find again", in
            the header, looks afresh once it is over.

        whileRunning:
            Running a target, the header gives its icon and name, and how it is
            going: a spinner and "Running", "Exited with 0" in the theme's
            success colour, "Exited with N" in its error colour, or "Stopped".
            Beneath it, its command, muted, in the monospace font, and then
            what it prints, its output and its errors together, in the order
            they come, a line each, in the monospace font on the theme's well
            surface, errors not told apart. The output is clean, as a terminal
            would show it, as the @{RunTargetsShape.consoleOutput} says. It scrolls with a
            @{ScrollbarScope} whose lock to the bottom starts on, following the
            latest output. The well runs beneath its scroll column too, so the
            column sits on the log's own surface, not the panel's base. A "Stop" button in the header stops it, and every
            process it started with it, while it runs; once it is over, a
            "Run again" button runs it afresh in its place.

        oneAtATime:
            One target runs at a time. Pressing the button of the target
            running brings back its panel. Pressing another's stops the one
            running and runs the other in its place. Finding the targets while
            one runs stops it.

        minimizing:
            Its minimize button's tooltip says the target keeps running, or
            that the search keeps going. While it runs, it is listed among the
            @{RunningActivityScope}, as "Running" then the target's name, or
            "Finding how to run". Closing the panel stops whatever it holds.

        switchingProjects:
            The panel belongs to its project, as the @{OpenProjectsScope}
            says: switching to another project minimizes it, what it holds
            carrying on in the background, and switching back brings it back
            minimized, just as it was left, the Code tab showing that
            project's targets and which of them runs. Each open project can
            run one target of its own at a time. Quitting doesn't ask, and
            stops every target running.

    consoleOutput:
        What a target prints is shown as a terminal would show it, never as
        the bytes it wrote. Its terminal escape sequences, those that colour
        text, move the cursor, clear the line, or set the window's title or a
        link, never show as text; neither do other control characters, nor
        bytes that aren't text. A line written over with a carriage return, as
        a progress bar is, shows as it was last written, a backspace takes
        back the character before it, and a tab lines up with the next tab
        stop, four columns along.

        It is highlighted as it would be in a terminal. Since its output isn't
        one, the command is asked for colour all the same, as the usual
        variables ask it, such as `CLICOLOR_FORCE`, `FORCE_COLOR`, and
        `CARGO_TERM_COLOR`, and the colours and emphasis it writes show: bold,
        dim, italic, and underline as themselves, and each colour as the
        @{ThemeScope}'s colour of its hue, never the terminal's own, so it is
        readable in both light and dark mode: red as the error colour, green as
        the success colour, yellow as the warning colour, blue as the accent,
        magenta as purple, cyan as cyan, black and white, and greys, as
        tertiary and primary text. A background colour is left out. A line
        written without colour that begins with `error`, `warning`, `note`, or
        `help`, followed by a colon or a bracket, has that word in the error,
        warning, or accent colour, as a compiler would colour it. A line is
        read once, as it arrives, never again as it is drawn.

    ribbon:
        In the ribbon's Code tab, a "Run" group. Until the project has targets,
        it holds a single full button, "Find How to Run", with a search icon,
        whose tooltip says the harness will look through the project to find
        how it is built, run, and tested. Once it has targets, the group holds
        a button for each, in the order saved, with its kind's icon and its
        name, whose tooltip gives its command: the first a full button, and
        primary, the rest slim. The button of the target running shows a
        spinner in place of its icon. Last, a slim "Find Again" button, with a
        refresh icon, looks afresh. Without a project, as the
        @{NoProjectStateScope} says, the group holds only Find How to Run,
        disabled, its tooltip saying to open a project to run it.

    shortcut:
        <Ctrl+F5> (<Cmd+F5> on macOS), anywhere in the window, runs the
        project's first target, its primary one, just as pressing its button
        does: while it already runs, it brings back its panel. Until the
        project has targets, it finds how to run it, as Find How to Run does.
        The tooltip of whichever of the two buttons it presses gives it. It
        does nothing without a project, or while an inset panel other than the
        Run panel is open.

        <Ctrl+Shift+F5> (<Cmd+Shift+F5> on macOS) runs the target marked
        release in the same way, and its button's tooltip gives it. Where the
        project has no release target, such as when it has no release build,
        or its targets were found before release ones were, it runs nothing,
        and a notification titled "No release run target" says so, and that
        Find Again looks for one, or that one can be marked in
        .suspense/run.json with "release": true.
        It is otherwise as <Ctrl+F5>.

content.text:
The spec already said Stop ends the target "and every process it started with it", but it never said how. The likely bug is that only the shell gets killed, so the npm → node → Vite chain under it keeps the server running. I added a section spelling out how the whole process tree is stopped. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 81 files, and it's under `.claude/reference/scope/run-targets/index.md#stopping`.

## What changed in the spec

New "stopping" section in `spec/scope/run-targets/index.pi`, under the panel's description:

- **Everything goes, however deep:** stopping a target ends its shell, what that runs, and every process those start. For example, `npm run dev` → npm → node → Vite and esbuild.
  - Dev servers, watchers and anything listening on a port stop with it.
  - The port is free once it reads "Stopped", so Run again never fails because the old server still holds it.
  - No process is left orphaned, on any platform.
- **How it's grouped:** on macOS and Linux the command starts in its own process group and session. On Windows it starts in a job object that every descendant belongs to.
- **How it's stopped:**
  - First it asks nicely, so servers can shut down cleanly: SIGINT then SIGTERM to the group on macOS and Linux, Ctrl+Break on Windows.
  - Anything still running 3 seconds later is killed: SIGKILL to the group, or the job is terminated.
  - Processes that left the group are found among the target's descendants and stopped the same way.
- **Honest status:** while it's stopping, the Stop button shows a spinner and is disabled. "Stopped" appears only once every process has exited.
- **Every way of stopping is the same:** running another target, finding targets, closing the panel and quitting all stop it this way. Nothing outlives Suspense.
- **Ending on its own:** if the target's command exits by itself, anything it left running in its group is cleaned up too.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791382870-StopServerOnButtonClick.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `RunTargetsScope`: `#stopping` for spawning in a group or job, the graceful-then-kill sequence and when "Stopped" shows, plus `#while-running`, `#one-at-atime` and `#minimizing` for the other ways a target is stopped.
- `ApplicationScope`: `#child-processes`, which still applies on Windows. A target's shell starts without a console window, even inside its job.
